comments.name: Integrity
comments.body: As a retired couples therapist, I would say that even a divorced couple can learn to collaborate for the sake of their children. As a nation, we have common interests. And the contempt of the Trumpian alliance is losing its allure for some former stalwarts as they and their kids become less able to afford the American dream.

comments.name: TheDiogenes..
comments.body: I have residences in a red state and a purple state. We interact socially on a frequent basis. I never,never hear contempt for the blue states nor for the liberal community. In addition I lecture on occasion at the universities business school. Again, in that environment there is no contempt for others. Admittedly, in some of our travels to the west coast and NYC i have heard some derogatory comments regarding the southern states, but it is infrequent. I am unaware of such contempt that we face a civil war. Perhaps the contempt is one sided.

comments.name: Miss Waterlow
comments.body: The marriage analogy cuts both ways. Fantasies of separation abound in marriages, but so does the hard work of repair. I believe Americans’ sense of contempt for one another is largely manufactured by media, including “influencers,” and political figures whom inculcating a permanent sense of rage benefits, either financially or for the assumption and retention of power. Repair is absolutely possible, but like a couple that values their union, Americans have to make the decision to do that work. It’s laziness to throw up our hands and continue to let ourselves be manipulated by whatever the opposite of “our better angels” is. We’re not helpless bystanders to our dissolution.

comments.name: ManhattanWilliam
comments.body:
It's easy to understand why many Americans keep imagining a new Civil War, not least because the first Civil War was never really settled.

The illusion that the Civil War ended racial discrimination and deep social divisions persists, but this is the false history we've been fed since 1865.  Jim Crow laws and other systemic segregation and discrimination existing to this day (not to mention the recurring tendency to embrace the Confederate Flag over vast swaths of the South), the ills upon which this country was founded have never been eradicated.  Add to this the current attacks on laws that were meant to address these ills like the Voting Rights Act which the current SCOTUS is determined to gut, and the problem not only perpetuates but seems to be worsening.

The Trump administration has had one consequence that it might not have intended but surely couldn't prevent:  the deep divisions within this country on which direction we should be going for a better future have never been more different, and these differences are mostly regional.  The federal system - the release valve -  that is meant to give states enough rights and sovereignty to provide us peaceful coexistence and prevent dissolution is breaking down.  The more the federal government attempts to restrict state laws, the worse the divisions and animosity become.

"New" Civil War?  Who can look at a map of the US today and see a unified country with shared values and a discernible desire to stay together.

comments.name: conordic
comments.body: I agree - the preconditions for a happy or even decent divorce do not exist in the US. When that has happened, like Sweden & Norway or Czekia & Slovakia, it has been question of clearly different peoples with different identities living in different pieces of land. The question has been: should we keep together or go separate ways? Moreover, there has been enough feeling of togetherness to rule out the use of violence to keep the country together. None of this exists in the US. Sorry.

comments.name: entity.z
comments.body:
yes there is deep, mutual contempt in our politics, but how deep is it?  It would be interesting to see polling on the feelings about separation. Not inviting a logistical analysis, we all know it would be complex.  I'm talking about the sentiment. 

I'm guessing the reds would be far more reluctant to separate than the blues. And that the reds would be more remorseful after the fact.

comments.name: BigWaveDave
comments.body: One of our intellectual disconnects is that "we" at once believe in the importance of our regional or value-based differences (Deep South versus everyone else, liberal versus conservative, costal elite versus middle rural), and our ingrained acceptance of our American Federalism. Drive around, do you see state flags or the Stars and Stripes? Is the chant "Iowa, Iowa, Iowa" or is it "USA, USA"? The idea of state sovereignty was answered as "NO" by The Civil War, and that answer has only become more accepted with time. What we need is a more responsive political system, and it's our constitution that is the problem.

comments.body: Can we learn something from others? Has there ever been a split of a nation into two mainly for political, not ethnical reasons? If so, did the resulting nations maintain significantly different political persuasions?

comments.body:
The tuition is too high.  It's crazy.

There's no reason to think about tweaking the system like this when the overall setup is so broken.  The times did a piece a few years ago about how most schools hire the same consulting firm that investigates families' finances and tells colleges how much they think students are able to pay, then they charge them that.

They set the sticker price extraordinarily high so that they can claim to be magnanimous when offering a discount but it's really just designed to extract as much money from every customer as possible.

Through that lens, it's not "merit" aid, it's really just the college saying, "hey, we know you could go to a better school than ours if you pay extra, but maybe take a discount to come here and pay a more reasonable price?"

The craziest part about all of this is these colleges pretend to be bastions of the progressive agenda when they are the most elitist, catering to the wealthy institutions in our entire country.

Want to fix college?  Get rid of all these aid shenanigans where you're pretending to offer deals but really just extracting as much cash as you can.  Offer everyone the same (reasonable) price - should be around 40k - and offer loans for those who can't afford it.

And Brian has heard it 100 times.100 years ago when life expectancy was 40 somebody might’ve asked him “why do  you want to live to your desired 75?”  The obvious point is lifespans are arbitrary and fluid throughout history and just because right now 75 seems like enough, there is nothing absolute about that.   That seemed ridiculous in the past just like 150 seems to him now. I can’t imagine how sad someone’s life is that they can’t find more things to contribute, more things to experience, more people to impact given more years of healthy life. If you are burned out with living by 75, don’t criticize someone else who feels there is more to live for and more to give.   It’s bad logic to equate someone wanting to live longer with making it all about them. If you’re selfish for the first 75 years, you’ll likely be selfish for the next 75 but if you’re a giving loving person who can contribute to society, there’s no reason that will stop. People need to stop thinking what they are used to has some inherent value that is superior to allot her options. History doesn’t work that way.  And neither does the future.

I think we are overtaxed generally.  Too much taxes for too much counterproductive and wasted government expenditures.

Except it turns out that the NYC property tax system has been gamed by special interests and under taxes some really expensive NYC real estate.  

The ultimate reason is because NYC property taxes hardly track property values.

Instead there is a byzantine framework that bifurcates the tax treatment of townhomes and traditional single family houses (very low tax) vs. apartment units structured as condos or coops (high tax in some neighborhoods).   

Property tax assessments heavily weight local market rents, and in doing so expressly take into account nearby rent regulated apartments.  In other words, government policy feeds back into government policy to lower the property tax rate in certain boroughs and neighborhoods.

Smaller walk ups generally are under taxed relative to value as well.  

The funny thing the group that is over taxed are rental landlords and tenants.  They pay, or indirectly bear, full bore property taxes.

The system creates huge disparities between neighborhoods, boroughs and blocks.  

The new pied a tier tax is just another layer of complexity on top of all that but at least is based on fair market value of the unit, regardless of these categories and loopholes.    

True reform will require a leader with A LOT more political capital than Mamdani.  Someone who could, gulp, double the taxes on brownstone Brooklyn.

Race, gender, wealth and social status are opaque and undetermined thus encouraging the formation of a just society.  This premise is foundational to any notion of the “common good”.  Regrettably it rarely applies in the world we live in.

comments.name: Gwen
comments.body:
Since I was too late to comment on other articles mentioning "Woke 1.0" I'm going to start by honing in on that first:

Whether or not "Woke 1.0 was crazy" as even AOC recently said, I don't think that everything that that period brought to our attention was wrong.  Without Woke 1.0, I probably never would have truly understood how my black colleagues across campus felt when they merely need to visit the supermarket or enter an academic networking situation.  In one case they receive too much unwanted attention, in the other none at all.  Without Woke 1.0, there would have likely been no accountability whatsoever by any police officer involved in any racist abuse of his force against an innocent black person.  I could go on and on about the many ways that Woke 1.0 brought some things into our awareness, but there is a character limit.

And, I concede that the problem with Woke 1.0 is not in its many correct observations but rather in *how* it went about solutions.  It was the implementation, the "corrective action", that was very rushed, overdone yet superficial, and just not really carefully thought through with the long term in mind.

To the more general topic: Likewise, with "common good", the underlying principles are essentially sound.  But, there is a disconnect going from principles to practice, even when said principles address social action: Such action is not uniquely defined for a given situation.  Yet, there are ways to "how" without violating another's "why".

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
The one thing I know is totally inimical to any possible conception of the "common good" is the execrable Citizens United decision - which clearly dictates that the Oligarchy (the wealthiest 0.0001 percent of all citizens) can simply purchase outright the government they desire - without a shred of regard for the wishes and rights of the vast majority of We the People.

After that, the next priority must be the elimination of all the inherent anti-majoritarian "poison pills" that slavery embedded into our two century-old Constitution: A Senate that gives twice the political power to the less than two million people in North and South Dakota than to the 40 million people in California, the abomination of unlimited gerrymandering and the deeply anti-democratic Electoral College.

Eliminate these utterly inexcusable (in any democracy) barriers to full political participation by ALL of We the People - and I suspect the rough and basic consensus of what constitutes the "common good" might suddenly become a lot more self-evident.

Libertarians want to disregard climate change and other evils that only government can solve. JD Vance wants to use the government to further fascism. comments.body: Up until September of 1978, I didn't think much of Bruce Springsteen. Sure, "Born To Run" was a great single on AM radio (all I had), but then the guy was gone for three years, which for a teenager is an eternity.  Then, picking up a Rolling Stone magazine only because it featured ELO, I read the cover story on Springsteen, written by one Dave Marsh. It was told over the course of several days in Hollywood: the band doing cannon balls in the Sunset Marquis pool, then jumping out to listen to a tape of the previous night's gig; a clandestine mission to deface a billboard of  "Darkness On the Edge of Town" (what band would do that??); Springsteen apologizing at a star-studded club show because regular fans couldn't get tickets. What Marsh brought to life was the passion, intensity, and sheer joy of Bruce and the E Street Band. Rock was more than glam and punk: it could be fun as well.  Over fifty shows later, I am highly indebted to Dave Marsh. To quote the last three words of the article: LET IT ROCK.

What was not made exicitly clear in this article is that the parking lot sits within a designated historic district, which is why approval was needed by the Landmark Preservation Commission. If the lot was around the corner, as is nearby 360 Bowery, a 22-story building, no review or approval by the LPC required.

If the zoning allows a big, tall building, a developer can build a big, tall building as of right. Generally, a proposal is put through an approvals process only when a change in zoning is requested, tax breaks are in the mix, or the site is within a historic district.

Some of the initial designs for 375 Lafayette were really out of character for the NoHo historic district and pretty terrible for any neighborhood in my opinion. 

The SOM design I saw was, and a version of which I assume was voted on, was pretty decent in terms of exterior design features, color, etc. Pulling in the look and feel of other nearby buildings. It's larger for sure, and to some perhaps out of scale, but to me it fits the neighborhood more than others recently built on the outside of the district edges.

It's baffling as to why an image wasn't included with the article or even a more detailed description given the main opposition was primarily related to aesthetics. 

I'm glad the plan was approved but to be clear, there is an argument to be had on the definition of affordable housing and the tax breaks given to developers.

The calculus is simple: is it safer for a ship to keep its transponder on, risking Iranian attack, or to shut it off and perhaps accept American Naval assistance in evading that attack?

The first year's syllabus was the nautical works of Joseph Conrad, and the discussions he led could have been mistaken for a graduate-level seminar.  His guidance was gentle and erudite, often sprinkled with his personal experiences from the sea.  

This first year set the tone, and the group continues to this day.  In the following years the group has read everything from "Moby-Dick" and "The Odyssey" to Ian Toll's histories to children's novels like Ransome's "Swallows and Amazons". Even better, most everyone who attends has actually done the reading.  Though Alzheimer's took John from leading and participating in the group a few years ago, his passing will undoubtedly weigh heavily when the discussions resume in September. comments.name: Johninnapa
comments.body: John was my watch captain on the Swan 47 Toscana for the 1979 Fastnet race. The yacht was owned by WW Norton senior editor Eric Swenson (they decided to do a book about the race before we finished). Our navigator was a retired British submarine commander by the name of John Coot. I have many vivid memories of the days of the race, but mostly the sense of confidence in the leadership of the team on that race. Terrifying hurricane strength winds and huge steep waves due to the relatively shallow Irish Sea for sure, but with these three in charge, I was never really scared for my life. The storm hit in the evening and howled all night, causing us to reduce sail significantly. The wind subsided a little by the next morning, when John reminded us we were still racing, and insisted we put up a headsail (which immediately blew out). I vividly recall the ashen concerned faces of the people standing on the old stone quay looking for their loved one’s boats as we sailed into Plymouth harbor. This was big news in the NY Times and my parents were able to find out that we were safe by calling the journalist that wrote the article. I remember walking through the streets of Plymouth the night we finished and seeing Ted Turner and his crew celebrating their victory in a fancy pub in town.

The Annapolis Book Of Seamanship was my bible and I can say it played a role in saving the lives of my son and me when we were caught in a “100 year storm” in 2015 on our sailboat in the Straight of Georgia. 

That killer storm came upon us a day sooner than any marine weather forecast had predicted. We were faced with being driven down on Cape Mudge, smashed to pieces and drowned.

Instead I found a way to claw up into the winds and seas for hours to gain enough sea room to finally get the storm on our stern and we were blown down alive and in one piece into Campbell River.

Everything I had learnt could be traced back to that book and my practical experiences. 

That book and Fastnet Force 10 informed my entire adult life as a sailor. I still have the boat, a modest 28-foot, full keeled, ocean-going packet cutter.

I am old enough now that it’s coming to the backstretch. This summer my son and I were on the boat and we just got back from what might be our last, long run on her.

There is a bookshelf below. On the shelf, not placed edge in, but face-out was my water-stained, tattered, a bit mildewed copy of the book. THE BOOK that is partly responsible for my being able to sit here writing this. 

The Annapolis Book Of Seamanship. 

I brought it home from Canada when we ended our run and it’s on the table in my office. 

And this morning, I read this. 

Well, thanks John. For helping to teach me how to feel freedom and live to enjoy it.

RIP old salt.

This is similar for other sports venues.  For Yankee Stadium and Met Stadium, NYC owns the underlying land and the NYC Industrial Development Agency (NYCIDA) owns the stadiums.

NYCIDA (New York City Industrial Development Agency) is owned by the City of New York.  It is a public benefit corporation of New York State, created under state law, but its board is controlled by the Mayor of New York City.

The mayor and other politicians are always talking about making the city “affordable.”  It would be nice if there were a provision in the leases that 5% of the tickets had to be affordable - perhaps $5 - so that a middle class or working family could attend events at public  facilities that many of the public cannot afford to attend.
